newsitem.title: KENYA: Ethiopian forces and Somali militia control border area.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopian forces and Somali militia control border area.

text.p: Ethiopian troops and Somali militia allies were in full control of an area inside Somalia on Friday after driving an Islamic fundamentalist group out of its stronghold, foreign aid and security sources said.
In Ethiopia's first comment, a foreign ministry official denied any involvement on Friday.

But the aid and security sources said there was no doubt that Ethiopian forces backed Omar Haji's Somali National Front (SNF) during the lightning offensive to capture the towns of Luq and Bulo Hawo in Gedo region.

"An Ethiopian helicopter brought Haji to Bulo Hawo on Thursday and there are reliable reports of Ethiopian armoured cars taking part in the attack," one of the sources in neighbouring Kenya told Reuters.
The sources said the offensive was aimed against Al-Ittihad Al-Islam (Islamic Unity), a Somali fundamentalist group.

Al-Ittihad's spokesman in Mogadishu, the Somali capital, confirmed on Thursday that the group's fighters had retreated from their stronghold at Luq, 100 km (60 miles) from the Ethiopian frontier in a remote area also bordering Kenya.
"The Ethiopians are holding the fort in Luq because the SNF are not strong enough to do that. But the majority of the force in Bulo Hawo are SNF," one aid worker said.
"The two towns have been calm since Thursday afternoon," she added. Luq was captured in the early hours on Thursday.

Ethiopia sent troops into the same area twice last year, calling al-Ittihad a "multinational terrorist group". Since last December Ethiopia had a military presence about 20 km (12 miles) inside Somalia but had not previously taken Luq.
All the foreign sources had heard rumours that the Ethiopian and SNF forces killed Afghani "Taleban" volunteers when they hit al-Ittihad training camps near Luq.
But there was no independent confirmation of those rumours which were sourced to Haji's SNF.
In Addis Ababa, a ministry of Foreign Affairs official told Reuters on Friday: "Ethiopia was not involved."
"Ethiopia has nothing to do with the current fighting inside Somalia," the official said.

Al-Ittihad set up its headquarters in Luq in 1992, a year after central government collapsed in the Horn of Africa country. Since 1991 Somalia has drifted through civil war and anarchy although most of the country is now relatively peaceful. There is no unified army to protect frontiers.

The lack of an internationally recognised government has meant that none of Ethiopia's incursions since August 1996 has drawn protests from the United Nations Security Council or the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
In Mogadishu, the self-proclaimed government of Hussein Aideed condemned what it called an intolerable and deliberate violation of Somali's territorial integrity.
Aideed spokesman Abikar Sheikh Hussein Qalli called on the U.N. and OAU to react to Ethiopian aggression.

But the deputy chairman of the rival faction led by Ali Mahdi Mohamed denied there was any foreign involvement in Gedo. Hussein Haji Ahmed Bod said the fighting was between the SNF and al-Ittihad which he accused of destabilising the Gedo region and of recruiting foreign Moslem militants.
Diplomats in the region say Ethiopia, whose population of nearly 60 million is split between Moslems and Christians, has long been alarmed by al-Ittihad's presence close to its border.
Islamic fundamentalists are suspected by the Addis government of responsibility for bomb attacks on soft targets like hotels during the past two years.
Al-Ittihad's fighters have retreated about 40 km (25 miles) from Luq to regroup at Yergud.
It was unclear whether al-Ittihad, led in Gedo region by Sheikh Mohamed Haji Yusuf, would counter-attack.
A foreign security source said Ethiopia had strengthened the SNF since Haji's militia failed to hold its positions last year against the Islamic militiamen.
"This time they've equipped them, put them in uniform and trained them," he said.
